correctness.rationale: The two Poisson marginal tails give the stated additive objective, even without joint independence. Its derivative has the sign of vy exp(B−2y)−1; this factor rises then falls, with its maximum at y=1/2 if the full positive half-line is considered. The stationary equation b_v(y)=B has its sole minimum at 1/2; each positive root satisfies B−y=y−log(vy)≥1, so any roots are interior. Up to the first stationary budget the objective strictly decreases except possibly at an isolated stationary point; above it only y=0 and the upper stationary point can maximize. Substituting stationarity into the value difference gives vH(y). Here H(0)=0, H′=(2y−1)e^(−y)(1−e^(−y)), and H(1)=1−3/e+1/e²>0, giving exactly one upper-branch zero u in (1/2,1). The strictly increasing upper branch therefore switches globally at b_v(u), with exactly the stated two allocations at the tie. Since y−B/2=(1/2)log(vy), equal effort occurs precisely at b_v(1/v)=2/v, strictly after the switch for v≤1. For fixed v and large B, the increasing solution has y=B/2+O_v(log B); substituting in the logarithm of the stationary equation gives the displayed next term and error.

value.rationale: The two-site problem is a natural minimal model of heterogeneous success thresholds. Its complete global classification isolates two different effects that local stationarity does not resolve: a value-independent positive entry dose while the entry budget varies, followed by the less valuable, harder target receiving the larger share. The exact split and thresholds supply a benchmark for more general resource-allocation models without claiming a field law.
residual_risks: The allocation result is restricted to the modeled visit tails and costs; it is not evidence for horticultural prescriptions or arbitrary many-flower extensions.
